title: Audio-Language Models: the Whisper to Audio Flamingo 3 Arc

questions.question: Why can a transcript-only Whisper-to-LLM cascade fail on questions about a song's mood or an explosion's timing?
options: The text model lacks a vocabulary entry for the word 'music'.
Transcripts lose acoustic cues and precise event timing.
The transcript contains too many visual patch tokens for the LLM.
The cascade cannot process any spoken words after transcription.
questions.explanation: A transcript preserves recognized words but generally omits acoustic properties such as musical timbre, vocal emotion, speaker identity, and precise sound-event timing. The vocabulary distractor blames missing word recognition, but the limitation remains even when the transcript is accurate because those cues are not words.

questions.question: A 30-second clip is represented at 100 log-Mel frames per second with 80 Mel bins. What feature-array shape results?
options: 3000 by 80, from 30*100 time frames and 80 bins.
300 by 80, from 30*10 frames and 80 bins.
30 by 100, from seconds and sample rate.
80 by 3000, from 80 time frames and 3000 bins.
questions.explanation: The feature array has time frames on its first axis and Mel-bin values on its second: 30 seconds × 100 frames/second = 3,000 frames, each with 80 bins. The 300-frame option uses 10 rather than the stated 100 frames per second.

questions.question: Which audio encoder does the lesson favor for music and environmental sound features that Whisper handles less well?
options: A CLIP image tower, trained on image-caption pairs.
Whisper's text decoder, trained only on vocabulary logits.
A VQ image tokenizer, trained on pixel reconstruction.
BEATs, trained self-supervised on AudioSet.
questions.explanation: BEATs is a self-supervised encoder trained on AudioSet, and the lesson contrasts its music and environmental-sound strength with Whisper's speech-dominant training. Whisper's text decoder generates recognized words; it is not an AudioSet-trained acoustic encoder.

questions.question: What does an audio Q-Former do between encoder frames and an LLM?
options: Learnable queries attend over encoder frames to summarize audio.
It expands each frame into a separate LLM layer with no compression.
It transcribes every frame into text and removes acoustic features.
It converts the LLM's output text into waveform samples.
questions.explanation: A fixed set of learnable queries cross-attends over the encoder's time frames and outputs a compact, fixed-length set of audio tokens for the LLM. The transcription distractor incorrectly turns the bridge into an ASR step and discards the acoustic representation it is meant to summarize.

questions.question: A product needs to identify instruments and speaker emotion, not just summarize spoken words. Which pipeline is better suited?
options: End-to-end audio-LLM, which preserves acoustic information for reasoning.
A text-only LLM that receives no audio or transcript.
Whisper transcription followed by a text-only summarizer.
A transcript cascade, because emotion is always explicit in words.
questions.explanation: Instrument identity and emotion are carried by acoustic properties that may not be spoken aloud, so end-to-end audio features give the model evidence a transcript omits. The option claiming emotion is always explicit in words confuses spoken content with vocal and musical cues.

questions.question: A podcast product only needs a text summary and has no music, emotion, or speaker-overlap requirements. Which choice follows the lesson's cost tradeoff?
options: Use a Whisper transcription followed by an LLM summary.
Use a full audio-LLM even though only words matter.
Use a Q-Former without a language model or transcript.
Use BEATs alone because it generates a text summary.
questions.explanation: When the requested output is only a summary of spoken content, Whisper can supply a transcript for a text LLM at lower cost and complexity than a full audio-LLM. The full audio-LLM option adds capability for acoustic-only reasoning the product explicitly does not need.
